title: Do All Buddhas Share One Dharma-body?
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: What does “The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body” mean? Is it from the Avatamsaka Sutra? Was it spoken by the Buddha?

inline.s: Question:
What does “The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body” mean? Is it from the Avatamsaka Sutra? Was it spoken by the Buddha?

Answer: The “one” in “one dharma-body” means “the same, without any difference.” “One dharma-body” means that the dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are identical to one another, without any difference. In Chinese, “one” is used to express
“the same”
, for example: “These flowers are not of one color.” The “one” in “one dharma-body” expresses that these dharma-bodies
are identical to one another
, without any difference. “In common” means that all are like this. “
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body
” means that the dharma-bodies of all Buddhas
are identical to one another
, without any difference.
In the three translations of the Avatamsaka Sutra—the “Forty-Fascicle Avatamsaka,” the “Sixty-Fascicle Avatamsaka,” and the “Eighty-Fascicle Avatamsaka”—there is no such sentence as
“The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body.”
Searching the entire Buddhist canon,
no sutra contains this sentence at all, still less was it spoken by the Buddha
Question: In the Avatamsaka Sutra
Chapter Ten, “The Bodhisattva Asks for Clarification,” the Bodhisattva Xianshou instructs:
“The bodies of all Buddhas are but one dharma-body, one mind, one wisdom-capacity; their powers and fearlessnesses
are likewise [one].”
This shows that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body, and do not
each
have their own dharma-body.
Answer: Here the
“but one dharma-body, one mind, one wisdom-capacity; their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise”
—the “one” means identical, without any difference: the dharma-bodies are the same, without difference; the minds, wisdom-capacities, and powers
(the ten powers)
and the fearlessnesses
(the four fearlessnesses)
are also the same, without difference. This is the same in meaning as “Mind, Buddha, and living beings—the three are without difference.”
[But one dharma-body] Here “but” is used at the head of the sentence and has no real meaning.
This is a usage of classical Chinese, for example:
“Ran Qiu’s [words]—are these not matters of state
(are not what Ran You (Qiu) spoke about matters of state)
(from the Analects,
the “Xianjin” chapter)

Mind, Buddha, and living beings—the three are without difference” means: the ultimate essence-nature of these three—mind, Buddha, and living beings—is identical, without any difference. Here “mind” refers to the self-nature (not the discriminating mind). And this ultimate essence-nature is the dharma-body. That is to say, the dharma-bodies of these three—mind, Buddha, and living beings—
are identical, without any difference
. The Avatamsaka Sutra (in sixty fascicles), Chapter Sixteen, “The Bodhisattvas in the Palace of the Yama Heaven Speak Gathas,” says:
“Mind, Buddha, and living beings—the three are without difference.”
If “all Buddhas share one dharma-body, and share the mind, wisdom-capacity, powers, and fearlessnesses,” then there would actually be only one Buddha—why then speak of “Buddhas” in the plural?

Moreover, if “all Buddhas share one dharma-body,” then, since they share one dharma-body they would be one and the same Buddha—what need would there be to go on to say that they “share the mind, wisdom-capacity, powers, and fearlessnesses”?
Moreover, in the Lankavatara Sutra, the Buddha says:
The dharma-body of me and of all the Buddhas
, along with the marks of the physical bodies,
are without difference
—except that, in order to tame living beings of the various different destinies, they manifest various different physical bodies,
this is called equality of body
Here the World-Honored One (Shakyamuni Buddha) instructs with utter clarity:
the dharma-body of me and of all the Buddhas is without difference; this is called equality of body.
This clearly is speaking of
the dharma-bodies of the Buddhas
being identical to one another
(equality of body)
, without any difference
. Where does it say that the Buddhas share one dharma-body?
Moreover,
the essential nature that has emerged from the shell of ignorance is called the dharma-body
for details see the answer to the next question, “What is the dharma-body?”
). And
the essential nature

is the original state of the self-nature. If “all Buddhas share one dharma-body,” that is to say, the Buddhas and living beings (living beings being future Buddhas) all have one and the same self-nature. Does this make sense? Shakyamuni Buddha restored his self-nature to the essential nature and thereby became a Buddha. If we shared one and the same self-nature with Shakyamuni Buddha, then our self-nature would likewise be restored to the essential nature, and we too would of course have become Buddhas—how could we still be the suffering beings of this evil world of the five turbidities?
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, one is a living being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”

I ask: this one self-nature shared by Buddha and living beings—is it deluded or awakened? If the one self-nature shared by Buddha and living beings is deluded, then all Buddhas would have become living beings; if this shared self-nature is awakened, then all living beings would have become Buddhas. Where then would the ten dharma-realms be?
Could this be so?!
[The ten dharma-realms] The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.

From this we know that to interpret “The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharma-body” and “The bodies of all Buddhas are but one dharma-body” as meaning “all Buddhas share a single dharma-body” is wrong.
Moreover, this is a fundamental error that will lead to a mistaken understanding of the entire Buddha-Dharma and to confusion in its doctrine! Its harm is immense.
Question: What is the dharma-body?
Answer:

The dharma-body is the true body of the Buddha, perfectly clear and pure, pervading the entire dharma-realm. The essential nature that has already emerged from the shell of ignorance is called the dharma-body; the essential nature still within the shell of ignorance, which stores the merits of all the Buddha-fruition grounds of the Tathagata, is called the tathagatagarbha (regarding the essential nature and the tathagatagarbha, see
Mind, Self-nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
). The Tathagatagarbha Sutra says:

“Just as the seed within the mango fruit is not destroyed, and when planted in the ground grows into a great king of trees—so too, good man! With the Buddha-eye I behold all living beings: the jeweled store of the Tathagata lies within the shell of ignorance, like a fruit-seed within its pit.
Therefore I teach the Dharma, opening up their tathagatagarbha, that they may swiftly attain the unsurpassed Way, as a fruit grows into a king of trees
(as a fruit-seed grows into a great king of trees)
Here the fruit-seed is a metaphor for the tathagatagarbha, and the great king of trees for the dharma-body.
The Srimala Sutra says:

“If one has no doubt about the tathagatagarbha wrapped in the store of countless afflictions, then one will also have no doubt about the dharma-body that has emerged from the store of countless afflictions.

(If a person has no doubt about the tathagatagarbha wrapped in the store of countless afflictions, then they will likewise have no doubt about the dharma-body that has emerged from the store of countless afflictions.)
......In this way, the Tathagata’s dharma-body, not yet separated from the store of afflictions, is called the tathagatagarbha
(the dharma-body not yet separated from the store of afflictions is called the tathagatagarbha)
The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The tathagatagarbha, pure in its self-nature, turns into the thirty-two marks and enters the bodies of all living beings, like a jewel of great price wrapped in soiled garments.”
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
“Suchness
(the essential nature)
while still wrapped is called the tathagatagarbha; suchness emerged from its wrappings is called the dharma-body.”
Master Mazu said:
“While wrapped it is called the tathagatagarbha; emerged from its wrappings it is called the pure dharma-body.”
(from the Extensive Record of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi)
Question: What are the three bodies?

Answer: The three bodies are the dharma-body (dharmakaya), the reward body (sambhogakaya), and the response body (nirmanakaya). The dharma-body is also called the self-nature body or the dharma-nature body; it is originally possessed by every person, but we living beings are deluded and so it is not manifest, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The reward body is formed from the Buddha’s wisdom and merits; it is divided into the reward body of self-enjoyment and the reward body for the enjoyment of others. The reward body of self-enjoyment is the body by which the Buddha himself enjoys the bliss of the Dharma inwardly realized; the reward body for others is the body manifested by the Buddha to teach the Dharma to Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The response body, also called the emanation body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of living beings.
